title: Difficult conversations and emotional distress
blurb: Break bad news, respond to distress and handle anger or complaints with compassion and honesty.
question: Mrs Adebayo, 66, has just been told her lung cancer has spread. After the doctor leaves she says quietly to the nurse, "I don't understand what he meant. Does this mean I'm dying?" What is the nurse's most appropriate response?

teach.body: A difficult conversation is any exchange where the news, the emotion or the conflict is hard for the person to hear or for you to deliver: bad news, an unexpected result, a mistake, an angry relative, a complaint. Annexe A 2.9 of the NMC proficiencies asks you to engage in these conversations, including breaking bad news, while conveying compassion. In plain English: don't avoid them, prepare for them, and stay human throughout.
teach.cite: NMC Standards of proficiency (2018) Annexe A 2.9; P1.12

teach.h: A six-step shape for breaking bad news

steps.label: Prepare
steps.sub: Private room, time protected, right people present

steps.label:
Find out what
they know
steps.sub: "What have you been told so far?"

steps.label:
Share in
small chunks
steps.sub: Plain words, warning shot, check understanding

teach.caption: Published frameworks such as SPIKES (Baile et al, 2000) follow this same six-step order.

teach.h: The Code clauses that anchor every difficult conversation
head: Clause
What it asks of you
rows: Respect how involved the person wants to be
Recognise anxiety or distress; respond compassionately
Share what they want or need to know, sensitively
Check understanding from time to time
Explain fully and apologise when things go wrong
A complaint must not affect the care given
teach.caption: NMC Code (2015, updated 2018).

teach.body: Start by asking what the person already knows and what they want to know. This tells you where to begin, exposes misunderstandings, and respects people who want less detail (Code 2.4). It is the person's information: a relative cannot decide that a patient with capacity should not be told (Code 5.5), but you can explore the relative's worries and let the patient lead. NICE NG31 makes the same point for prognosis: discuss it unless the person does not wish to.

teach.h: Scenario: Mrs Adebayo on the respiratory ward
teach.body: Mrs Adebayo asks, "Does this mean I'm dying?" The nurse sits down, makes sure the curtains give privacy and asks, "Can you tell me what you understood from the doctor?" She listens, then answers honestly in plain words at the pace Mrs Adebayo sets, pausing to let her react. She does not guess at a timescale she cannot know; she offers to bring the doctor back to answer that, and records the conversation so the team can follow up (Code 10.2).

teach.h: Responding to distress: helpful versus unhelpful

rows.label: Silence
values: Fill it with facts or chatter

teach.h: An angry relative or a complaint

steps.label: Stay calm
steps.sub: Move somewhere private; mind your own safety (13.4)

steps.label: Listen fully
steps.sub: Let them finish; don't interrupt or defend

steps.label: Acknowledge
steps.sub: Name the feeling and the concern

steps.label: Act and record
steps.sub: Fix what you can, escalate, document

teach.caption: Use complaints as feedback for reflection and learning (Code 24.2).

teach.text: Reassurance is not the same as compassion. "Don't worry, you'll be fine" closes the conversation and may be untrue. Acknowledging the feeling ("This is a lot to take in") and staying with the person is the compassionate response. And a complaint about you never changes the standard of care you give that person (Code 24.1).

teach.h: When distress hides something more serious
items: Listen for hopelessness: "What's the point?" or "Everyone would be better off without me".
Ask directly and compassionately about thoughts of self-harm or suicide; it opens the door to help.
Do not use a risk score to decide what happens next (NICE NG225); focus on needs and immediate safety.
Escalate to the team and, where needed, mental health services; record what was said.
Prepare: privacy, time, the right people (Code 5.1 privacy).
Find out what they know and how much they want to know before telling (Code 2.4).
Plain words, small chunks, check understanding (Code 7.1, 7.4).
Respond to emotion with silence, acknowledgement and presence (Code 2.6).
Angry people: listen, acknowledge, apologise, act, record; complaints never affect care (Code 24.1).

summary: You can now prepare for and lead a bad-news conversation in a person-centred order, respond to distress with presence rather than empty reassurance, and handle anger and complaints in line with the Code. You can also spot when distress needs a direct question about suicide.

A.q: A doctor is about to tell Mr Kowalczyk, 59, that his biopsy shows cancer. The nurse will be present. Which preparation is most appropriate?
options: Book a quiet room and hand over her bleep for the meeting
Hold the discussion at his bedside with the curtains drawn
Ask his son to come so the news can be given to him first
Prepare a leaflet so he can read the results before they meet
A.why: Breaking bad news well starts with preparation: a private space and protected time so the conversation is not interrupted (Annexe A 2.9; Code 5.1 privacy, 2.6 compassion).

whyNot.1: Curtains do not give acoustic privacy on a ward; other patients can hear, so a private room is better.
whyNot.2: Mr Kowalczyk has capacity and the information is his; family are involved as he wishes (Code 5.5).
whyNot.3: Learning a cancer diagnosis from a leaflet removes the chance to support him and answer questions.

A.q: Before giving Mrs Lindqvist, 71, the results of her scan, the nurse wants to understand where to begin. Which opening is most appropriate?
options: "The scan has shown something we need to talk about."
"What have you been told so far about why you had the scan?"
"Would you like me to call a relative before we start?"
"Are you worried that the scan result is going to be cancer?"
A.why: Finding out what the person already knows shows where to start, reveals misunderstandings and lets her set the pace (Code 7.4 check understanding; Code 2.4).

whyNot.0: A warning shot has a place, but opening with it skips finding out what she already understands.
whyNot.2: Offering support is reasonable, but it does not tell the nurse what Mrs Lindqvist already knows.
whyNot.3: This is a closed, leading question that introduces 'cancer' before the nurse knows what she understands.

A.q: After hearing his heart failure is worsening, Mr Osei, 82, falls silent and his eyes fill with tears. What is the most appropriate response from the nurse?
options: Explain the treatment options so he can focus on the plan
Tell him that many people live well with heart failure for years
Stay with him, allow the silence and acknowledge how he feels
Offer to come back later when he is feeling a little calmer
A.why: Code 2.6: recognise distress and respond compassionately. Allowing silence and acknowledging feelings shows presence and gives him space to process the news (Annexe A 2.9).

whyNot.0: Moving straight to treatment detail while he is distressed means the information is unlikely to be heard.
whyNot.1: General reassurance dismisses his feelings and may not be true for him.
whyNot.3: Leaving at the moment of distress withdraws support when he needs it most.

B.q: Ms Fraser shouts at the nurses' station that her mother has been waiting an hour for pain relief. What is the nurse's most appropriate first response?
options: Explain that the ward is short-staffed and very busy today
Ask her to lower her voice before the matter is discussed
Give her the details for the trust's complaints service
Listen, acknowledge her concern and apologise for the wait
B.why: Listening and acknowledging defuses anger, and Code 14.2 asks you to apologise when things go wrong. The nurse then acts on the pain relief and records the concern.

whyNot.0: Explaining staffing first sounds defensive and does not address her mother's pain.
whyNot.1: Asking her to calm down before listening tends to escalate anger rather than reduce it.
whyNot.2: She can be told how to complain, but signposting first avoids dealing with the concern in front of you.

B.q: Mr Brennan, 63, has capacity and is awaiting biopsy results. His wife asks the nurse to make sure he is not told if it is cancer. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Agree, as relatives often know best how a patient will cope
Explore her worries and explain he will be asked what he wants to know
Tell her the results will be given to her first so that she can decide
Explain that he must be told everything as soon as results arrive
B.why: The information belongs to Mr Brennan, who has capacity (Code 5.5). Exploring his wife's fears is compassionate, and asking him how much he wants to know respects his choice (Code 2.4).

whyNot.0: Withholding information from a person with capacity at a relative's request breaches Code 5.5.
whyNot.2: Sharing his results with his wife first, without his agreement, breaches his confidentiality.
whyNot.3: People differ in how much they want to know; forcing full detail ignores Code 2.4.

B.q: Mr Hale has made a formal complaint about Nurse Priya's manner. He remains on her ward and is allocated to her today. What does the Code require of Priya?
options: Swap patients so a colleague cares for him until it is resolved
Continue to give him the same standard of care as before
Limit contact with him to essential care tasks for now
Wait for her manager's advice before she speaks to him
B.why: Code 24.1: never allow someone's complaint to affect the care provided to them. Code 24.2: use complaints as feedback for reflection and learning.

whyNot.0: Reallocation is a management decision, not a Code requirement, and avoiding him changes his care because of the complaint.
whyNot.2: Reducing contact to tasks alters his care because he complained, contrary to Code 24.1.
whyNot.3: His care cannot pause while she waits; she should continue to care for him professionally.

C.q: At 02:00 Mr Ahmed, 58, recently diagnosed with motor neurone disease, is awake and tearful. He says, "What's the point of going on?" What is the nurse's most appropriate response?
options: Reassure him that the team will keep him comfortable throughout
Suggest he talks this through with his consultant on the morning ward round
Offer a hot drink and something to help him settle back to sleep
Sit with him, explore what he means and ask about thoughts of suicide
C.why: His words may signal hopelessness. Exploring them and asking directly about suicidal thoughts supports him (P1.12, Code 2.6) and allows escalation; NICE NG225 focuses on needs and immediate safety.

whyNot.0: Reassurance without exploring what he means may miss suicidal thoughts.
whyNot.1: Deferring to the morning leaves a possible risk unexplored overnight.
whyNot.2: Comfort measures are kind but do not respond to what he has just disclosed.

C.q: A doctor needs to tell Mrs Haddad, 74, who speaks Arabic and little English, that her husband has died. Her 15-year-old grandson offers to translate. What should the nurse arrange?
options: A professional Arabic interpreter for the conversation
Her grandson, with the doctor speaking slowly and simply
A bilingual healthcare assistant from another ward
A written note in Arabic followed by the conversation
C.why: NHS England interpreting guidance (2018): offer a professional interpreter; using under-16s is unacceptable except for immediate necessary treatment. Code 7.2 requires reasonable steps to meet language needs.

whyNot.1: A 15-year-old should not interpret, and certainly not to deliver news of a death to his grandmother.
whyNot.2: Staff who are not trained interpreters may translate inaccurately in an emotionally complex conversation.
whyNot.3: Learning of a death from a written note is not compassionate and gives no chance to respond.

C.q: During a family meeting, Mr Lennox's daughter becomes increasingly angry, stands up and moves towards the nurse, shouting. What is the nurse's most appropriate action?
options: Stand her ground and explain the care plan in a firm, louder voice
Keep a safe distance near the exit, speak calmly and get support
Ask the daughter to leave the hospital until she can be calm
End the meeting and tell the family it will be rearranged
C.why: Code 13.4: take account of your own safety. A calm voice and space reduce escalation, and calling colleagues ensures support if the situation worsens.

whyNot.0: Matching her volume tends to escalate confrontation.
whyNot.2: Excluding a relative is a last resort and does not deal with the immediate risk.
whyNot.3: Ending abruptly may inflame her further and leaves the concern unresolved.

reteach.title: Think of it as walking alongside, not delivering
reteach.question: If breaking bad news is less like handing over a parcel and more like walking someone through a door, what does the nurse do at each stage?

blocks.body: You don't push someone through a door; you check where they are standing (what they know), ask whether they're ready (how much they want), go through together a step at a time (small chunks), stop when they need to (emotion), and agree where to go next (plan). The Code supplies the rules: respect their level of involvement (2.4), share what they want or need (5.5), use plain words (7.1) and respond to distress compassionately (2.6).

blocks.text: Silence feels awkward to the nurse, not to the grieving person. Resist filling it.

explain.body: Choose a private room, protect the time (hand over your bleep), and have the right people present, including an interpreter if needed. Privacy is part of dignity (Code 5.1) and makes it easier for the person to react.

test.q: Which setting is most appropriate for telling Mrs Bell, 60, about an unexpected diagnosis?
options: A quiet side room with time protected
The bay, with curtains drawn round
The ward corridor near the station
The day room while other patients are out
test.why: A private room with protected time gives privacy and space to respond (Code 5.1, Annexe A 2.9).

whyNot.1: Curtains do not stop others overhearing.
whyNot.2: A corridor is public and interruptions are likely.
whyNot.3: Others may return at any moment, so privacy is not assured.

explain.body: Ask what they already know and how much they want to know. Then share information in small chunks, in plain words, checking understanding as you go (Code 7.1, 7.4).

test.q: Partway through explaining a diagnosis, the nurse notices Mr Dunn looks confused. What should she do next?
options: Repeat the full explanation more slowly
Continue and offer a leaflet at the end
Pause and ask what he has understood so far
Ask a relative to explain it all to him later
test.why: Code 7.4: check people's understanding from time to time. Asking shows exactly where the confusion lies.

whyNot.0: Repeating everything does not identify what he has misunderstood.
whyNot.1: Carrying on adds more information he may not absorb.
whyNot.3: Passing the task on leaves his confusion unresolved now.

explain.body: Allow silence, name the feeling ("This is a lot to take in"), and stay. Avoid false reassurance or rushing to the plan. Code 2.6: recognise distress and respond compassionately and politely.

test.q: A woman begins to cry after hearing her test result. Which response best conveys compassion?
options: "Try not to upset yourself, it may be fine."
"I can see this is very hard to hear."
"Let me explain what happens next."
"Shall I fetch you a cup of tea?"
test.why: Acknowledging the feeling validates her distress and keeps the conversation open (Code 2.6).

whyNot.0: This dismisses her feelings and offers reassurance that may be false.
whyNot.2: Moving to the plan during strong emotion means it is unlikely to be heard.
whyNot.3: A kind gesture, but it steps away from her distress rather than acknowledging it.

explain.body: Listen without interrupting, acknowledge the concern, apologise for what went wrong (Code 14.2), act and record. A complaint never changes the care you give (24.1); use it for reflection (24.2). Keep yourself safe (13.4).

test.q: A son complains angrily that his father's meal was left out of reach. What should the nurse do first?
options: Explain that the meal was delivered by catering
Advise him to put the complaint in writing
Tell him she will look into it after the drug round
Listen to him fully and acknowledge his concern
test.why: Listening and acknowledging first defuses anger and shows the concern is taken seriously; an apology and action follow (Code 14.2).

whyNot.0: Shifting responsibility sounds defensive and does not help his father.
whyNot.1: Signposting to a written complaint first avoids dealing with the problem now.
whyNot.2: Delaying leaves both the meal and his concern unaddressed.
